corrected_draft.title: HHS Begins Mass Layoffs Across Health Agencies
corrected_draft.description_short: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs across HHS agencies, including FDA, CDC and NIH; Reuters reported plans to cut 10,000 staff.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On April 1, 2025, the Trump administration began mass layoffs at several Department of Health and Human Services agencies, including the FDA, CDC and National Institutes of Health. Reuters reported that the cuts were part of a plan to reduce HHS headcount by 10,000. The reporting supports a broad health-agency reduction, not the entry’s specific claim that DOGE fired 1,500 NIH scientists in March.
corrected_draft.description_long: Reuters reported that the Trump administration began mass layoffs at U.S. health agencies on April 1, 2025, after employees received dismissal notices. The cuts affected several agencies under HHS, including the FDA, CDC and National Institutes of Health, and were part of a plan reported to reduce HHS staffing by 10,000. Reuters cited multiple sources and described staff losses involving drug regulation, vaccine research, public health, and other functions. At NIH, Reuters reported that institute director Jeanne Marrazzo was fired from her post and offered another position in the Indian Health Service. The report also described staff laid off at CDC, including at least one person working on the federal measles response. It does not establish that DOGE fired approximately 1,500 NIH scientists and researchers in March or that this was one-sixth of NIH’s workforce. The substantiated event is the April 1 start of broad HHS agency layoffs.

corrected_draft.title: Trump Urges Supreme Court to Limit Nationwide Injunctions
corrected_draft.description_short: On March 20, 2025, Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ power to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration actions.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ ability to issue nationwide injunctions against administration actions. Reuters reported that Trump posted “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW” and that the Justice Department had asked the Court to narrow injunctions blocking his birthright-citizenship order. This supports a specific challenge to nationwide injunctions, not a claim that Trump denied courts all authority over the executive branch.
corrected_draft.description_long: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump called on the Supreme Court to limit federal judges’ authority to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration policies. Reuters reported that Trump made the appeal in a social-media post, writing “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW,” and that the Justice Department was separately asking the justices to narrow three nationwide injunctions against his birthright-citizenship order. The cases involved courts in Washington state, Massachusetts and Maryland. Trump’s statement concerned the scope of injunctions that apply beyond the parties before a court. The available reporting does not say that he declared federal judges had no authority to constrain or review the executive branch. Reuters also reported that federal courts were hearing more than 100 lawsuits against administration initiatives and that the Supreme Court’s six-member conservative majority included three Trump appointees. Injunctions against earlier presidents had also been issued. The event should be described as a call to curtail nationwide injunctions and related Supreme Court litigation, not a rejection of judicial review generally.

corrected_draft.title: DOJ Challenges Maryland Court’s Automatic Immigration Injunctions
corrected_draft.description_short: On June 25, 2025, DOJ announced a complaint challenging a Maryland court standing order that automatically enjoined some immigration removals.
corrected_draft.description_medium: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland over a standing order requiring automatic injunctions when detained people filed habeas petitions. DOJ said the order blocked removal or challenges to their legal status and characterized the practice as judicial overreach. The release documents a legal challenge, not a refusal to obey court orders.
corrected_draft.description_long: On June 25, 2025, the Justice Department announced that it had filed a complaint against the U.S. District Court of Maryland concerning the court’s standing order on immigration habeas petitions. According to DOJ’s release, the order instructed the court clerk to automatically enter an injunction against removing or challenging the legal status of a person detained in Maryland who filed a habeas petition. The department argued that the standing order conflicted with the requirements for preliminary injunctions and with Supreme Court precedent. Attorney General Pamela Bondi said that injunctions had impeded President Trump’s agenda and described the Maryland order as judicial overreach. The public statement documents DOJ’s formal challenge to a specific court procedure and its criticism of the judiciary. It does not establish that Bondi refused to enforce multiple injunctions, as the original entry claimed.
